title: Your rebrand failed the moment you wrote the brief
caption:
"Modern, clean, premium but approachable."

We've read that brief a hundred times.
And it could fit a hundred other brands.

Here's what usually happens.
You sit down to write a brief. Maybe you ask ChatGPT to help.
And you write what you THINK is right for your brand.
It sounds good. It feels "Good Enough".

The studio reads it. Nods. Delivers exactly that.
And months later you're looking at something that matches the brief perfectly... and isn't you at all.

That brief didn't help you THINK about YOUR brand.
It just described a brand. Any brand.

For us, a brief is a translation of a translation.
Every hand-off loses a little more of what you meant, especially once it gets to the UX-UI.

That's why we do it a bit differently.
We DON'T start from a brief.
We start from your strategy, your positioning and your growth plan.
Real questions. Visual examples on the table. UX options.
Then we give you a prototype to play with, so you react to the real thing, not to a paragraph about it.

So... next time someone asks you for a brief,
ask for a strategy based conversation instead.

title: The Duo
caption:
People always ask us who does what.

Short answer...
Keren on strategy. Amir on UX-UI and design.

Real answer...
Keren walks into a project asking "what makes you different, for real?"
Positioning. Messaging. Where the business is going.
Amir walks in asking "so what happens when someone clicks here?"
Flows. Screens. A prototype you can actually play with.

Two different questions.
And that's exactly the point.

Most studios split this into two teams and a hand-off.
Strategy goes one way, design goes the other, and somewhere in between your brand turns... generic.

For us, it's one table.
The strategy pushes the design. The design exposes the gaps in the strategy.
Back and forth, until it's precise.

Otters hold hands while they sleep, so they don't drift apart.
That's us.
And that's what we do with your brand.

Say hi in the comments, we'd love to know who's here

title: The Spiral, how we work
caption:
Here's a question we ask on almost every first call...
"When was the first time you actually SAW your last project?"

The answer is usually the same.
At the end.
After the brief, after design, after the build. When changing anything meant paying for it twice.

That's the straight line. It looks tidy on a Gantt chart.
It's also where brands quietly turn generic.

For us, it works in a spiral.
We start from the end, where the business is going, what people should understand and do, and from day one, strategy, UX and a clickable prototype move together.

You click. You react.
We loop back sharper.
Again. And again.

Every loop, the UX exposes gaps in the strategy, and the strategy gives the design a clearer job.
So by the time we're done, there's no big reveal.
You've been inside your product the whole way.

Speed isn't the goal. Precision is.
Speed is just what happens when you stop guessing.

Save this for your next project

title: Case study, day one to launch
The Nomad, two cities one project
caption:
When Amir wakes up in Berlin, Keren is already at lunch in Koh Phangan.
Sounds like a recipe for chaos, right?
Missed messages. "Wait, who has the latest version?" Decisions made while someone was asleep.

Turns out, it's the opposite.
By the time Amir opens his laptop, the strategy and positioning decisions from Keren's morning are waiting for him.
By the time she's back, there are new UX flows and screens waiting for her.
Your project keeps moving while one of us sleeps.

What makes it work isn't the time zones.
It's that we never hand off and walk away.
Strategy and UX-UI live on the same table, move together, and check each other every single day.

And for you? One team. One strategy. One version of the truth.
You don't need to know which island we're on.

Where are you reading this from?
Tell us in the comments.

title: Behind the scenes, a real moment
caption:
No fancy studio. No sticky-note wall staged for the camera.
Just this.

Last week a client asked us to use the analogy of "Teach them to fish, don't give them the fish".
We weren't thrilled about it. Keren thought that this generic idea won't go with the brand's strategy. Amir thought that adding this idea to the design is going to result in a non-premium look.

This is the part nobody sees.
The moment between "here's what I want" and "oh... we're NOT doing that to your brand".

But this is where a strategic conversation comes handy.
Asking the strategy questions, and sharing the consequences for choosing something over something else.

Who is this really for?
What makes it different?
Where is the business going?

Amir is already turning the answers into UX options, rough, fast, clickable.

A few loops like this, and a generic brief becomes a product you can actually play with.

Not magic.
Just strategy and UX-UI on the same table, so your brand never ends up... "Good Enough".

title: AI didn't kill design
caption:
Hot take...
AI didn't kill design. It exposed who never had taste.

For years, "it looks good" was enough to sell a design.
Now anyone can generate a good-looking screen in seconds.
Which means good-looking isn't the value anymore.
It's the starting point. And it usually looks like everyone else.

The real value is the part AI CAN'T do for you.
Looking at 50 options and knowing which one is right, for this business, this positioning, this growth plan.
And knowing why.

That's taste.
And taste is really just strategy with a lot of hours behind it.

We use AI every day. It makes us faster.
But speed without strategy just gets you to "Good Enough"... faster.
So for us, strategy decides, UX decides, and AI speeds up everything else.

So... did AI make design better or worse?
We want to hear it in the comments

title: 3 signs your brand is "Good Enough"
caption:

title: Your brand isn't a logo, it's a world
Demographics vs what your client actually feels
caption:
"Our audience is business owners, 35-50."
Okay. But which ones?
The ones who just raised their prices and need a site that matches?
The ones who got burned by their last agency?
The ones who have a board meeting in 3 weeks?
Same age. Same income. Completely different conversation.

That's why, for us, a persona is built around urgency: what's pressing, what they've tried, what they're afraid of getting wrong this time.
And the only way to know that is to actually talk to them.

When your brand is built on that, people feel it.
When it's built on a spreadsheet, they feel that too.

So, people or data points?
Tell us in the comments.

#brandstrategy #branddesign #uxui #positioning #designstudio #targetaudience #customerresearch

title: "Authentic" means nothing
Brand strategy vs creative strategy
caption:
"Can we see some design options?"

We love that question. Just not in the first meeting.
Because design options without a clear brand strategy are guesses.
Pretty guesses. Sometimes very pretty.
But nobody can say which one is right, because nobody has decided what "right" means yet.

Brand strategy decides who you're for and what makes you different.
Creative strategy decides how that looks, sounds and moves.
And for us, UX-UI sits in between, because the way people move through your brand is part of the message.

So, is your brand strategy clear, or still a work in progress?
No judgment. Tell us in the comments.

title: What we'd tell you about your brand over coffee
caption:

title: Don't let AI make your brand "Good Enough"
caption:
You can't prompt your way to differentiation.

We say this as a studio that uses AI every day.
It speeds up our research, our drafts, our prototypes.
But it never decides who the brand is.

Because AI is built on what already exists.
Ask it for a brand, and it gives you the most likely answer. The average. The "Good Enough".
And your clients have already seen that brand a hundred times.

So do it in the right order.
Strategy and positioning first, the human part, the part where we dig out what's actually true about you.
Then let AI do what it's great at.

Where do you draw the line with AI in your business?
Tell us in the comments.

title: Please don't make it another swirl
caption:
Scroll through the AI category for 30 seconds.
Swirl. Spark. Another swirl. A slightly purple swirl.

We get it. It's a new category and everyone wants to look like they belong in it.
But that's the problem.
When everyone looks like they belong, nobody stands out.

That's what positioning is for. Figuring out how to stand out in your category, not blend into it.

For us, it goes like this.
Step 1: map the category. Who's out there, what they say, how they look.
Step 2: find what's actually different about you.
Step 3: build the brand, the UX and the visuals around that.
Step 4: don't make a swirl.

Building something new?

title: Your brand walks into a cafe
caption:
Your brand, as a person, walks into a cafe. What happens next?

We love this question because nobody answers it with "modern, clean and professional".
People get specific. Fast.
And specific is exactly what a brand personality needs.

Then comes the uncomfortable part.
Put that person next to your homepage. Do they sound the same?

If they don't, it's not a copy problem. It's a strategy problem: your brand knows who it is, but your site hasn't been told yet.

So what's your brand ordering?

title: Logo vs Branding, a real example
caption:
Your logo is one piece of a much bigger picture.

On our biggest project so far, the logo wasn't where the work started.
It started with 8 conversations with their clients, and the question behind every one of them: why do people really choose them?

That became the positioning. The positioning became one line.
And that line became a whole world: their client as the whale, the brand as the sonar that finds the depth.

Then the UX-UI, built as a story from the first scroll to the last CTA.
And a colour palette that refused to play it safe.

That's branding.
Not how it looks. What it means, every time someone meets it.

title: Trends are not a strategy
caption:
Every year, the trend lists come out.
And every year, a few brands jump on one, then look dated 18 months later.

We have nothing against trends.
Some of them are beautiful. Some of them might even be right for you.
But "right for you" is a strategy question, not a Pinterest question.

For us, the visual style comes last.
First we figure out who you are, who you're for, and what makes you different.
Then we pick the look that says that, trendy or not.

So which one are you tempted by?
Tell us, and we'll tell you honestly if it fits. (Said with love.)

#brandstrategy #branddesign #uxui #positioning #designstudio #designtrends2026 #trendsvsstrategy

title: How to build a brand people remember
Your UI doesn't need 8 colors
caption:
More color doesn't make a product feel more alive.
Usually it just makes it louder.

In UI, color has a job. It points. It says "this one". It tells people what matters on the screen.
And when 8 colors are all pointing at once, nobody knows where to look.

The fix isn't only a design decision though.
Your main color should live on your most important action, and knowing which action that is, is strategy.
That's why, for us, UX-UI and strategy are never two separate phases.

How many colors are on your homepage right now?
Be honest. Tell us in the comments.
